newsitem.title: USA: UAL pilots seek to fly regional jets.
newsitem.headline: UAL pilots seek to fly regional jets.

text.p: The pilots' union at UAL Corp's United Airlines Friday reaffirmed its position that it wants United's mainline pilots, not commuter airline pilots, to fly any new regional jets the airline would buy.
The issue of which pilots would fly the regional jets has become a sticking point in United's plan to purchase regional jets that would feed its hub operations and add service to smaller markets.

In a recorded message for its union members, United's Air Line Pilots Association said "Whereas the regional jet issue is of great significance and importance to the future of the pilots of United Airlines ... the (union's master executive council) reaffirms its position that any jet operated in the United livery or used to provide to passenger feed to the UAL operation under any form of relationship to the UAL Corporation will be flown by pilots on the UAL seniority list."
It said its negotiating committee is expected to enter talks with United management to resolve the issue.
Any agreement reached with management would be submitted to the union membership for ratification, the union said.
United representatives were not available to comment.

Last week, United Chairman Gerald Greenwald told the Washington Post he expected a solution would be reached with the pilots' union to allow commuter carriers to fly regional jets as part of the United Express system.
Several commuter airlines operate under the United Express name. These airlines are not owned by UAL but use the brand name under a marketing agreement.

Conflict about regional jet flying has rippled throughout the airline industry. Many carriers see regional jets as an inexpensive way to compete with low-cost carriers. The issue was a major stumbling block in the bitter labor negotiations at AMR Corp's American Airlines.
United Airlines is a unit of UAL Corp. United's employee own 55 percent of its common stock.
